transcript:
<header>
Date: 2026-12-19
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Ravi Patel (Redwood SE); Ava Martinez (Neptune Dir. of ML); Liam O'Connor (Neptune ML Eng); Priya Shah (Neptune Infra)
</header>

Summary: Short technical deep dive to troubleshoot repeated KV cache evictions under Neptune's production workload and discuss mitigations (paging, prefetch, sharding, prefix reuse).

Topics: KV eviction patterns; paging strategies; long-context workloads; batching tradeoffs; quantization interactions; VPC/networking for Private deployment.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. quick intro - I'm Maya, AE on this account, and Ravi from our infra team will run through the KV cache traces you sent.
[00:16] Ava Martinez: Hi, thanks. we've been seeing spikes in token latency and some sessions lose prefix context - leads to hallucinations in the assistant. timeline: started after we switched to longer convo windows in November.
[00:30] Ravi Patel: Right. we pulled the eviction logs you shared, and there are repeated LRU-style evictions at around 9-11GB used per device. seems like working set growth + some large one-off requests evicting many entries.
[00:46] Liam O'Connor: yeah, I think our assistant sometimes sends a long attachment-like prompt, it's basically a 6k token system message that triggers paging.
[01:02] Priya Shah: To be clear we're on your Dedicated plan with 2x A100s per pool, VPC peering, private subnets, and local NVMe enabled. Network's fine, it's the cache behavior we're worried about.
[01:18] Ravi Patel: Couple of high-level angles: eviction policy tuning (LRU vs segmented LRU), increasing on-device cache, or enabling KV paging to host memory and prefetch heuristics. each has tradeoffs.
[01:34] Ava Martinez: Can you explain paging to host memory? does that add significant latency?
[01:42] Ravi Patel: Good question. Paging moves older KV shards off GPU DRAM to host RAM (or NVMe) and rehydrates on miss. if we page to host RAM it's typically tens to low hundreds of ms on a miss; NVMe can go seconds if not cached. Pre-fetching frequently-hit prefixes reduces misses.
[02:00] Maya Chen: Also there was a note in the logs about prefix reuse - some prefixes like the persona prompt are identical across sessions but stored multiple times because of tokenization differences.
[02:14] Liam O'Connor: yup, we saw duplicate keys due to whitespace/trailing tokenization differences - that's on our side but curious if Redwood can dedupe.
[02:26] Ravi Patel: We can normalize tokens at ingest and apply a canonicalization step for prefix keys. cheap fix: strip trailing spaces and collapse duplicate prefixes before KV insert; better: hash canonicalized string as key.
[02:40] Ava Martinez: Would that risk changing behavior for clients that rely on exact token sequences?
[02:46] Ravi Patel: We make canonicalization optional and plumb it via model config; default is conservative. we can run tests to show parity.
[02:58] Mia (automated transcript note - misheard): "we can run the replay" — uh
[03:04] Maya Chen: (laughs) yes, run the replay. Speaking of which Neptune agreed to run a replay harness to reproduce eviction, right?
[03:10] Ava Martinez: yes, we'll run the same traces. timing: want results by next week. we also want to see tail latency impact.
[03:22] Ravi Patel: On eviction policy: plain LRU is simple but can thrash with large one-off contexts. seg-LRU or a tiny frequency counter helps keep hot prefixes. we've had success with seg-LRU + a small protected queue for persistent prefixes.
[03:38] Liam O'Connor: when you say protected queue, how many entries are reasonable? our hot set is roughly 200-300 prefixes during peak.
[03:46] Ravi Patel: For your working set I'd suggest reserving ~5-10% of on-device KV capacity for protected entries, plus a TTL-based policy to evict truly unused ones.
[03:58] Priya Shah: Any change to cache allocation affects GPU memory for model params; we can't exceed device memory. thoughts on offloading other things like activations or quantizing to free up room?
[04:12] Ravi Patel: Quantization can help reduce KV footprint marginally if keys/values are stored in lower precision; but note KV is mostly raw embeddings/activations depending on model. Compression primitives (8-bit or 4-bit) for KV are experimental and can slightly increase CPU cost to decompress on miss.
[04:30] Liam O'Connor: Could batching help? we currently do micro-batches at 16 requests per step, which adds some latency but improves throughput.
[04:40] Ravi Patel: Batching helps amortize compute, but it increases the KV cache pressure because more concurrent contexts are live. For tail-latency sensitive workloads, you might reduce batch size or route low-latency traffic to a dedicated pool with larger KV reservation.
[04:56] Maya Chen: We should also talk about prefix reuse across users. if many sessions share system prompts, we can centralize those prefixes in a shared read-only namespace to avoid duplication.
[05:10] Ava Martinez: That sounds promising. Any security implications for shared prefixes in a multi-tenant setup?
[05:18] Ravi Patel: For hosted/shared deployments you'd only share non-sensitive system prefixes. For Dedicated/Private we can guarantee isolation; shared namespace can be per-tenant with deduping at ingestion.
[05:30] Liam O'Connor: On the logs you mentioned eviction hotspots are they due to sequence length distribution or due to occasional long requests?
[05:38] Ravi Patel: Both. Your histograms show a long tail: 70% of requests are under 512 tokens, but 5% exceed 4k tokens and those are the culprits. When a 4k request allocates a big KV footprint, it pushes out multiple hot entries.
[05:54] Ava Martinez: Is there an approach to cap per-request KV footprint so one request can't evict everything?
[06:02] Ravi Patel: Yes, per-request KV caps and soft quotas. we can reject or spill-to-host when a request would allocate beyond a threshold. That keeps the working set stable but may increase misses for the large request.
[06:18] Maya Chen: Priya, would you be ok with a soft cap approach for now while we run the replay and confirm behavior?
[06:24] Priya Shah: yes, we'd prefer not to silently increase latency for other customers; soft caps with graceful fallback sound fine.
[06:32] Liam O'Connor: What's the expected latency from spilling to host RAM vs NVMe? we run some real-time UIs that can't tolerate >200ms tail.
[06:40] Ravi Patel: Host RAM page is typically 20-150ms depending on concurrency and NUMA. NVMe is 500-2000ms in worst cases. So if your tail SLO is 200ms, NVMe is not acceptable for hot misses; host RAM can be borderline.
[06:56] Maya Chen: We should also consider prefetch heuristics. e.g., when a session opens, we prefetch the most probable prefixes into GPU RAM based on hinting from the client.
[07:08] Ava Martinez: we can add a hint header with top-k expected prefixes would Redwood accept that in the request metadata?
[07:14] Ravi Patel: Yes, we support optional prefix-hint headers. SE can provide instrumentation to measure prefetch hit-rate.
[07:24] Liam O'Connor: Another thought: sharded KV across devices if we increase number of GPUs, does that reduce per-device eviction because working set spreads?
[07:34] Ravi Patel: Sharding helps but adds cross-device rehydration cost. If you have a consistent hashing scheme and most requests touch a small subset of shards, you can achieve scale-out with acceptable tail latency.
[07:46] Priya Shah: For on-prem deployment, what are the networking constraints for paging to host RAM across nodes? Is that supported or do we prefer local host RAM per GPU node?
[07:56] Ravi Patel: Our paging currently is local to node host RAM; cross-node paging is possible but we'd need to ensure RDMA and low-latency fabric; otherwise it's too slow.
[08:10] Maya Chen: On quantization you mentioned compression for KV. does that interact badly with prefix equality checks?
[08:18] Ravi Patel: We only compress values; keys remain canonicalized strings/hashes. compression shouldn't affect equality but may affect latency on rehydration due to decompress CPU cycles.
[08:30] Ava Martinez: Are there recommended observability metrics we should track to detect upcoming eviction events?
[08:36] Ravi Patel: yes: per-device KV utilization (GB), eviction rate (entries/s), spill-to-host rate, miss rate, per-prefix popularity, tail latency p95/p99 for rehydrated requests. we'll send dashboards.
[08:54] Maya Chen: We'll attach a dashboard template to the follow-up email.
[08:58] Liam O'Connor: One more prefix reuse: if tokenization differences cause duplicates, is there a way to normalize at the tokenizer layer? we have multiple tokenizers in our pipeline.
[09:08] Ravi Patel: Canonicalization has to be aligned to the model tokenizer used in serving. mismatch causes different keys. we recommend normalizing to the serving tokenizer; SE can provide a small library to do that.
[09:22] Priya Shah: For the pilot, we'd prefer it to run in our VPC with Private deployment. are there limits on host RAM paging or capacity planning docs?
[09:30] Maya Chen: Redwood Private supports host RAM paging; we'll share capacity planning and best practices doc.
[09:36] Ava Martinez: Great. can we get an ROI estimate do any of these mitigations affect cost materially?
[09:42] Ravi Patel: Tradeoffs: increasing GPU memory or adding GPUs ups infra cost; paging to host RAM is cheaper but increases tail latency risk; dedupe/canonicalization is low-cost. We'll model cost in the pilot proposal.
[09:58] Maya Chen: Let's wrap with concrete next steps and owners.
[10:02] Ravi Patel: Action items: I'll run the replay on Redwood side with the sample traces you upload and instrument eviction logs; tweak seg-LRU with protected queue and measure.
[10:12] Ava Martinez: We'll send traces and the tail SLO doc by EOD Monday 2026-12-21.
[10:18] Maya Chen: I'll send SOC2 + network diagram + dashboard template today. propose pilot config once we see initial replay results.
[10:24] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. thanks everyone.
[10:28] Priya Shah: Thanks.

End of call.

References shared: /links/replay-trace.zip (Neptune); Redwood KV-eviction-playbook.pdf; benchmark-sheet.csv
